title: Perrin's Tunnel Triumph
markdown:
Perrin was a fine canal otter, sleek and quick, whiskers twitching with a curious spark. He could snatch a minnow faster than a blink. He had a secret, jelly-kneed: enclosed spaces. A narrow log made his whiskers vibrate like nervous tuning forks. A hollow tree? A prickly sensation, ants under the fur.

His best pal, Sol, was a maintenance orb: grapefruit-sized, one big friendly eye pulsing helpful light. Sol knew every bolt and pipe. He whizzed, zapped leaks, hummed metallic tunes like a tiny robot choir. Dependable as a well-built dam.

"Perrin, my pal!" Sol trilled one afternoon, eye blinking. "Deep in the old Northwind Tunnel: a bloom of Lumina Algae! It glows like a thousand fireflies having a party in the darkest water!"

Perrin's tail twitched, nerves. Dark. Long. Enclosed. "The… tunnel?" Thin voice. A shiver. The algae was rare; Sol needed it for a peckish water-sprite. The clock ticked. A giant stone hatch sealed the tunnel at sundown. Shadows were already creeping.

"We've got to race a barge through! Loaded with supplies! Only way there and back before the hatch slams. Before the last ray disappears!"

A barge. A tunnel. The hatch. Minnows cartwheeling in Perrin's tummy. Whiskers drooped. He thought of the sprite who would go peckish without the glow, and of Sol's one hopeful eye, and of the way the canal always looked wider when you were about to leave it. He nodded, braver than a damp teabag, for Sol, for the glow.

They loaded the barge with barrels and crates, the air filling with oak and something vaguely like pickled onions. Sol counted the load twice. Perrin counted his own breaths. Neither number was as large as the tunnel. Perrin shoved, trying not to think of the dark ahead. As they nudged into the canal Sol buzzed, "Here's where it gets tricky. Wider water here, then the tunnel's a squeeze. Keep your nose pointed straight. And if you hear a drip that isn't us, it's the tunnel talking to itself. Perfectly normal. Mostly."

They glided toward the mouth. The Northwind yawned like a shadowy maw. Whiskers quivered, sensing the shift. Air grew heavy. Light shrank to a sliver. Everything sounded different: a faint drip-drip from deep within, water colder, as if it had sat in a forgotten icebox. Perrin's fur wanted the reeds and the wide bright reach. He pointed his nose anyway.

Whoosh. The barge dipped, listed. Crates slid, barrels tumbled, clatter off unseen walls. Perrin yelped, claws scrabbling. Fear of being trapped, squeezed under dark cold water, surged like a rogue wave. "Sol! It's tipping! We'll sink!"

Sol zipped, a steady beacon. "Easy. Buoyancy. Weight distribution. Too much on one side, the water's upward push lists us. Shift those barrels. The heavy one — other side. Quick!"

Paws fumbled. Heart a frantic drum. Rough wood, damp moss, musty forgotten things. "I can't! Too heavy! So dark!"

"You can. Think about the algae. The glow. Lighting your burrow."

A heavy clunk, a grinding screech. A rusted ancient sluice jammed, blocking the path. Sol probed rusty gears. "Stuck fast! Needs a shove from the other side, where the mechanism is. Tight squeeze, Perrin!"

Into the dark narrow gap, tight even for a shrew. Fur prickled. Cold sweat. Chill water in his paws, stagnant air. Stuck. Exactly what he dreaded.

But Sol was counting on him. That soft steady glow, an island in oppressive dark. Deep shaky breath, cheeks puffed. He paddled into the murky gap, fur brushing slimy cold stone, pushed with all his might, cold metal biting his paws. Scrape. Grate. CLUNK. The gate groaned like an ancient giant clearing his throat and swung inward, revealing a slightly wider passage. Water slapped the stone in a new, more hopeful rhythm.

He scrambled back, panting, heart still a rabbit's foot, a strange new feeling mixed in. He had done it. Pushed through. Just a little. Sol did a small loop that, in orb-language, was applause.

As they continued, walls seeming to press closer, Sol pointed ahead. "Look! Light!" A faint greenish luminescence flickered. Perrin felt a surge of hope, a spark in his chest. The exit? As they drew closer he saw it was not open sky but a patch of strange ethereal fungi clinging to the wall, pulsing with eerie light, casting odd shadows. The tunnel felt longer now, darker; the weight of stone made his breathing shallow. The desire to turn back — familiar sunlit canal, reeds swaying, clear water — was overwhelming. "Sol," he whispered, words catching. "Maybe we should just go back. It's too scary."

Sol's eye swivelled, glow softening. "We're so close. Don't you want to see the Lumina? The firefly party?"

Perrin looked at that unwavering optimism. He remembered the glow, the reason. He remembered the gate, cold metal, scrape. He had not let Sol down then. He would not now. A steadier breath.

"No. We're not going back." He looked at the barge, the shifting crates. Buoyancy. He could use that. He nudged barrels, redistributing, a new understanding. The barge settled, stable. He steered with a confidence that surprised him. Fear still a whisper, no longer a roar.

Walls seemed to recede. A fainter current of wider canal. Then a sliver of bright daylight. The exit. But the massive stone hatch was already descending, a low ominous rumble through the water.

"Faster, Perrin!" Sol's light on the dwindling gap.

Narrowing. Whiskers barely twitching. He steered at the closing hatch, fur on end, thrill not only fear. Rumble overhead, damp chill, spray on his nose. The barge wanted to yaw; he corrected the way Sol had taught him, nose pointed, barrels still where he had put them. A crate slid an inch and stopped. He focused on the sliver of day, not on the stone coming down.

CRASH.

Through. Brilliant sunshine. The hatch slammed behind them, a final echoing thud. Nick of time. Water exploded into light. Reeds slapped the hull as if congratulating it. Lumina Algae, safely stowed, shimmered in the hold, a soft ethereal promise. Sol spun a full circle and then another, light bright enough to make the wet barrels look festive.

Perrin looked back at the dark silent tunnel, then at Sol, pride and relief in that one eye. He had delivered the algae. He had also delivered himself. On the open canal he let the barge drift a moment, just to feel width, just to hear ordinary birds instead of drip-drip. That night he slept, and dreamed not of dark tunnels but of bright glowing wonders. In the morning he batted a loose reed near the burrow — a narrow obstacle he had once avoided — and went past it without a speech about being stronger. The reed, unimpressed, swayed. The canal went on being wide.
